f1.title: OpenAPI Spec Editor
f1.deck: The outline follows the specification's real structure, not a guess based on indentation. Navigate paths and components as a tree, and fix errors where they live.
f1.b1Body: Validate against the 3.0, 3.1 or 3.2 dialect your file actually declares.
f1.b2Body: Jump to definitions, inspect usages, and get suggestions for misspelled references.
f1.b3Body: Your repository remains the source of truth.
f1.b4Body: CI failures and editor diagnostics speak the same vocabulary.
f2.title: API Debugging Against Your Spec
f2.deck: A request builder shaped like the tools developers already use, plus one thing those tools cannot do by default: verify responses against the contract.
f2.b1Title: Collections generated from paths and tags.
f2.b1Body: No import step and nothing to manually re-sync.
f2.b2Body: Detect undeclared properties, missing fields and type drift inline.
f2.b3Body: Reuse existing development and staging configurations.
f2.b4Body: Bearer, API key and OAuth configuration starts from the specification.
f3.title: Generate an MCP Server from OpenAPI
f3.deck: Your specification is already a tool manifest. Powerduck compiles it into a runnable MCP server and shows exactly which OpenAPI fields produced each tool.
f3.b1Body: Every tool traces back to its operation, operationId and schema.
f3.b2Body: Missing metadata is visible instead of silently producing weak tools.
f3.b3Body: Change the specification and tools update without a build step.
f3.b4Body: Run through stdio or HTTP for local agents and workflows.
f4.title: API Documentation from the Same Contract
f4.deck: Reference documentation generated directly from your OpenAPI model, exported as static files and hosted wherever you want.
f4.b1Body: Required flags, enums and descriptions stay synchronized.
f4.b2Body: Generate cURL, Node, Python and Go examples from operations.
f4.b3Body: Success and error responses come from the same objects your debugger validates.
f4.b4Body: No runtime dependency and no documentation platform lock-in.

faq.title: Questions developers ask first
faq.deck: The practical details around local files, OpenAPI versions, MCP generation and licensing.
faq.q1: Does Powerduck upload my OpenAPI specification anywhere?
faq.a1: Your project remains local. AI requests send selected source context to Powerduck’s managed model providers. Publishing documentation is a separate action you choose.
faq.a2: OpenAPI 3.0, 3.1 and 3.2. Powerduck detects the declared version and validates against the appropriate dialect instead of using a lowest common denominator.
faq.q3: How does the MCP server get generated?
faq.a3: Operations with an operationId become MCP tools. Arguments are derived from parameters and requestBody schemas. Component schemas can be exposed as resources. The generated server updates whenever the specification changes.
faq.q4: How do subscriptions and credit resets work?
faq.a4: Powerduck uses monthly subscriptions. Free credits reset daily; paid credits reset every seven days.
faq.q5: Can I keep using Postman collections?
faq.a5: Yes. Existing collections and environments can continue to be used. Powerduck treats the OpenAPI specification as the authoritative contract and helps identify where requests drift from it.
faq.a6Before: Yes. The same validation and generation engine is exposed through
faq.a6After: , a CI-ready command-line tool that runs during pull requests and automated pipelines. It supports batch testing across 6 protocols (HTTP, SSE, WebSocket, gRPC, MCP, GraphQL), configurable concurrency, and JUnit-compatible reports for CI integration.

flow.hero:
Your agent writes the code.
Powerduck handles the API.
flow.sub: Give Codex, Claude Code or Cursor the API contract. Turn code into docs, run business scenarios with AI, and check real results — from a local-first API workspace.
flow.title: Each familiar chore becomes a contract-driven flow.
flow.baseTitle: Local work should not mean a stripped-down workspace.
flow.baseBody: Sign in to open your local workspace. Keep your project files on your machine; selected context is sent to Powerduck’s managed AI when you request analysis.
flow.difference: What would you like to stop doing manually?
flow.1.pain: Do you still read the source code to find out whether the API docs are right?
flow.1.title: Generate docs from the project.
flow.1.body: Scan a supported project from your coding agent through MCP. Generate an API definition and open it as documentation.
flow.1.result: A reviewable API definition + a local docs link.
flow.1.prompt: Scan this project and give me an API documentation link.
flow.2.pain: Have you given AI the spec, only to get different fields and paths back?
flow.2.title: Implement from the actual API contract.
flow.2.body: Connect your coding agent to Powerduck’s MCP. Let it read the actual paths, schemas and auth before implementing, then verify the running API.
flow.2.result: Implementation guided by the contract, checked against real responses.
flow.2.prompt: Implement this API from its definition, then run contract tests.
flow.3.pain: Do you manually repeat the same business flow after every API change?
flow.3.title: Run the whole business scenario.
flow.3.body: Describe a flow such as sign in → create an order → retrieve it. Let AI compose the scenario, pass values between steps and execute the test.
flow.3.result: Step-by-step results and failed assertions, not just a generated test script.
flow.3.prompt: Test sign in → create an order → retrieve it. Show which step fails.
flow.4.pain: Do you switch tools just because the next endpoint uses a different protocol?
flow.4.title: Inspect seven protocols in one place.
flow.4.body: Debug HTTP, GraphQL, WebSocket, SSE, gRPC, MCP and A2A. Inspect responses, streams and tool calls in the same workspace.
flow.4.result: Manual control when you need to inspect exactly what happened.
flow.5.pain: Do you copy requests and responses into chat every time you need AI’s help?
flow.5.title: Investigate with real request context.
flow.5.body: Give the assistant the relevant API context. Ask it to send a request, inspect the response and help narrow down the failure.
flow.5.result: A diagnosis grounded in request results, with changes you can review.
flow.5.prompt: Investigate why this request fails. Check the response before suggesting a fix.
flow.6.pain: Do you maintain a separate hosting setup just to share API docs and MCP?
flow.6.title: Publish docs and MCP from one API.
flow.6.body: Publish a version of your API to Powerduck Cloud. Give people readable docs and give AI clients an MCP endpoint.
flow.6.result: Hosted documentation and an MCP URL, without running your own hosting stack.

scenes.s1.note: Supported frameworks only. Review inferred fields and scan warnings. Local links work on the MCP host while its session is running.
scenes.s3.note: Checks cover the operations, inputs and assertions you run. They do not prove every behavior of the backend is correct.
scenes.s8.note: Protocol support differs between desktop and browser. Use the desktop app for native transports such as gRPC.
scenes.s5.note: AI features require a configured model. Context sent to a remote provider leaves your device; manual editing does not require AI.
scenes.s6.note: Cloud hosting uses your account quota. The uploaded API definition may contain examples or internal details: review it before sharing.
